analysis.one_liner: Repeals Depression-era limits on utility holding companies, replacing strict oversight with lighter rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 24 cosponsors in June 1996, the bill never got a committee vote and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 tightly restricted how electric and gas companies could structure themselves, after decades when layered holding-company pyramids hid costs from regulators and drove up rates. This bill repeals that law and replaces it with a much lighter one: the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and state regulators could still inspect the books of holding-company affiliates and reject affiliate costs charged to utility rates, but the old structural limits on sprawling corporate pyramids and non-utility businesses would disappear. Anyone already exempted under the old law would stay exempt. The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and its two relevant subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Electric and gas utility holding companies gain the most. They would be freed from Securities and Exchange Commission registration and from the 1935 act's limits on corporate structure, letting them merge, restructure, and branch into other businesses without federal approval. Companies already exempted under the old law would have those exemptions locked in [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 1935 act, which required holding companies to register with the SEC and restricted utility systems to a single integrated geographic area and connected businesses [S2] [S3].

Replaces it with oversight limited to transactions that affect utility rates: FERC and state commissions can access holding-company books and decide whether affiliate costs may be recovered in rates, but there is no regulation of structure, mergers, or non-utility activities [S2] [S3].
Carries forward every exemption previously granted under the 1935 act, and lets FERC grant new exemptions whenever it deems regulation irrelevant to rates [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Utility ratepayers bear the risk. The 1935 act was passed because holding-company pyramids had layered costs onto customer bills; this bill removes the structural limits that kept companies transparent and simple, leaving rate reviews as the only check. If regulators miss an inflated affiliate charge, customers pay it in their rates. The SEC's utility-regulation office and records would be transferred to FERC [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 1935 act's core protection was structural: it could not be evaded by how a company organized itself, because the SEC policed the structure itself. The replacement only polices transactions that visibly affect rates, so a holding company could diversify, merge, and grow without any federal review as long as its dealings with the utility look clean on paper [S2] [S3].
FERC could exempt any person or transaction it deems irrelevant to rates, after consulting state commissions — a broad door for carving regulated companies out of even the lighter rules [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off: the bill preserves state and federal access to affiliate books and rate review, but rate protection then depends entirely on regulators detecting disguised costs in complex corporate structures — the exact problem the 1935 act was written to prevent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is not a total giveaway: it keeps state commissions' access to holding-company records and keeps both federal and state authority to strike affiliate costs from rates, which the 1935 act did not provide to states in this form [S3]. But the headline change — repealing structural limits on utility holding companies in exchange for transaction-level review — shifts the burden of proof onto regulators and ratepayers. The cost side is the risk that complex corporate structures once again hide costs from view, which is precisely the abuse the 1935 act was enacted to stop.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Commerce Committee and its subcommittees from June 1996 until Congress ended in January 1997, never getting a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Billy Tauzin and eight other members introduced the bill on June 6, 1996, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce [S1] [S3] [S5].
On June 21, 1996, it was sent to two subcommittees — Telecommunications and Finance, and Energy and Power — splitting jurisdiction over it [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action was the subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the 1935 act stayed in force and utility holding companies remained under the SEC's structural rules. State regulators and ratepayers kept the existing protections; the holding companies did not get the deregulation they sought in this Congress.

for.name: Rep. W.J. (Billy) Tauzin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up 24 cosponsors

against.name: House Committee on Commerce
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; after splitting it between two subcommittees on June 21, 1996, took no further recorded action

sides.party_line_note: 20 of the 24 cosponsors were Republicans and 4 were Democrats; the bill never reached a vote, so there are no roll calls to show how the full chamber would have split.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utility holding companies
industries.note: The bill repeals the 1935 act's structural limits, freeing holding companies to merge, restructure, and enter other businesses without SEC approval. Its gains come from reduced oversight of exactly the affiliate transactions that feed into customer rates.

The bill gives state commissions explicit access to holding-company books, which they lacked in usable form under the 1935 act. But they would lose the SEC as a federal backstop policing company structure, leaving them to police costs alone.
The bill transfers the SEC's utility holding-company oversight functions, records, and staff to FERC, ending the SEC's role as the regulator of utility holding companies [S2] [S3].
